title: Microsoft Confirms Windows 11 25H2 UI Features Broken also Along With 24H2 Following Update
raw_text: Microsoft Confirms Windows 11 25H2 UI Features Broken also Along With 24H2 Following Update gbhackers. Wednesday, December 3, 2025 Linkedin RSS Twitter gbhackers. Home Threats Cyber Attack Data Breach Vulnerability What is DFIR Top 10 Search Follow us On Linkedin Microsoft Windows 11 25H2 UI Features Cyber Security News Microsoft Windows 1 min. Read Microsoft Confirms Windows 11 25H2 UI Features Broken also Along With 24H2 Following Update By Abi naya December 3, 2025 Share Facebook Twitter Pinterest WhatsApp Microsoft has acknowledged a significant issue affecting Windows 11 versions 24H2 and 25H2. Where critical user interface components break following the installation of monthly cumulative updates released on or after July 2025. The problem impacts XAML dependent modern applications, including core Windows components such as File Explorer, the Start menu, System Settings, Taskbar, and Windows Search. Users in affected environments may experience a range of disruptive symptoms, from applications failing to launch to complete desktop rendering failures. Overview of the Windows 11 UI Breakdown Issue Microsoft confirmed that this issue primarily affects enterprise and managed environments. Stating it is “very unlikely to occur on personal devices used by individuals.” The bug manifests in specific provisioning scenarios. Particularly when Windows updates are installed before the first user logon to a persisted operating system installation. In non persistent environments such as virtual desktop infrastructure (VDI) deployments. In VDI scenarios, application packages must be installed during each logon session, making these environments especially vulnerable to the timing related registration failure. Affected users may encounter several critical failures. Explorer.exe crashes can cause users to log on to a black screen with no visible taskbar. The Start menu may fail to open entirely, often displaying a critical error message. System Settings silently fails to launch, and other XAML dependent applications crash during startup when attempting to initialize XAML views. The root cause is that XAML dependency packages fail to register in time after a Windows update is installed. The affected packages include Microsoft Windows. Client.CBS, Microsoft.UI.Xaml.CBS, and Microsoft Windows.Client.Core. While Microsoft works on a permanent resolution, IT administrators can implement manual workarounds. For persistent installations, administrators should register the missing packages using PowerShell’s Add AppxPackage command and restart SiHost to allow Immersive Shell components to initialize correctly. For non persistent VDI environments, Microsoft recommends implementing a logon script approach using a batch file wrapper. This ensures the registration script runs synchronously, effectively blocking Explorer from launching prematurely until required packages are fully provisioned. Microsoft stated that they are actively developing a resolution and will provide updates as more information becomes available. has acknowledged a significant issue affecting Windows 11 versions 24H2 and 25H2.</p> <p>Where critical user interface components break following the installation of monthly cumulative updates released on or after July 2025.</p> <p>The problem impacts XAML dependent modern applications, including core Windows components such as File Explorer, the Start menu, System Settings, Taskbar, and <a href="https://gbhackers.com/clickfix attack/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">Windows Search.</a></p> <p>Users in affected environments may experience a range of disruptive symptoms, from applications failing to launch to complete desktop rendering failures.</p> <h2 class="wp block heading" id="h overview of the windows 11 ui breakdown issue"><strong>Overview of the Windows 11 UI Breakdown Issue</strong></h2> <p>Microsoft confirmed that this issue primarily affects enterprise and managed environments.</p> <p>Stating it is “very unlikely to occur on personal devices used by individuals.” The bug manifests in specific provisioning scenarios.</p> <p>Particularly when Windows updates are installed before the first user logon to a persisted operating system installation.</p> <p>In non persistent environments such as <a href="https://gbhackers.com/android and chrome virtual cards/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">virtual</a> desktop infrastructure (VDI) deployments.</p> <p>In VDI scenarios, application packages must be installed during each logon session, making these environments especially vulnerable to the timing related registration failure.</p> <p>Affected users may encounter several critical failures. Explorer.exe crashes can cause users to log on to a black screen with no visible taskbar.</p> <p>The Start menu may fail to open entirely, often displaying a critical error message.</p> <p>System Settings silently fails to launch, and other XAML dependent applications crash during startup when attempting to initialize XAML views.</p> <p>The root cause is that XAML dependency packages fail to register in time after a Windows update is installed.</p> <p>The affected packages include Microsoft Windows. Client.CBS, Microsoft.UI.Xaml.CBS, and Microsoft Windows.Client.Core.</p> <p>While Microsoft works on a permanent resolution, IT administrators can implement manual workarounds.</p> <p>For persistent installations, administrators should register the missing packages using <a href="https://gbhackers.com/shuckworm group leverages gammasteel/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">PowerShell’s</a> Add AppxPackage command and restart SiHost to allow Immersive Shell components to initialize correctly.</p> <p>For non persistent VDI environments, Microsoft <a href="https://support.microsoft.com/en us/topic/kb5072911 explorer the start menu and other xaml dependent apps might not start or close unexpectedly on some enterprise devices d2d30684 4e2b 47f5 9899 a00a8e0acb09" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener nofollow">recommends</a> implementing a logon script approach using a batch file wrapper.</p> <p>This ensures the registration script runs synchronously, effectively blocking Explorer from launching prematurely until required packages are fully provisioned.</p> <p>Microsoft stated that they are actively developing a resolution and will title: Let’s Encrypt Cutting Certificate Lifespan from 90 Days to 45 Days
raw_text: Cutting Certificate Lifespan from 90 Days to 45 Days gbhackers. Wednesday, December 3, 2025 Linkedin RSS Twitter gbhackers. Home Threats Cyber Attack Data Breach Vulnerability What is DFIR Top 10 Search Follow us On Linkedin Let’s Encrypt Certificate Lifespan 45 Days Cyber Security News 2 min. Read Let’s Encrypt Cutting Certificate Lifespan from 90 Days to 45 Days By Divya December 3, 2025 Share Facebook Twitter Pinterest WhatsApp Let’s Encrypt, the nonprofit certificate authority serving millions of websites, announced a significant shift in how it issues digital certificates. Starting in 2026, the organization will reduce the validity period of its SSL/TLS certificates from 90 days to 45 days, with complete implementation expected by February 2028. The move aligns Let’s Encrypt with broader industry standards mandated by the CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements, which establishes technical guidelines for all publicly trusted Certificate Authorities. This industry wide initiative aims to strengthen internet security by limiting the scope of potential compromise and improving the effectiveness of certificate revocation. Beyond shortening certificate lifespans, Let’s Encrypt is also reducing its authorization reuse period from 30 days to just 7 hours by 2028. This means domain control validation will need to occur more frequently. However, the organization is introducing new tools to streamline this process. A Phased Rollout to Minimize Disruption Rather than implementing changes overnight, Let’s Encrypt will deploy updates across multiple stages using ACME Profiles, which give administrators control over when to adopt new standards. The timeline includes three key milestones. On May 13, 2026, the organization will launch its TLS server ACME profile for early adopters and testing, issuing 45 day certificates. The following year, on February 10, 2027, the default classic profile will issue 64 day certificates with a 10 day authorization reuse period. Finally, on February 16, 2028, the classic profile will fully transition to 45 day certificates with a 7 hour authorization reuse window. Most Let’s Encrypt users with automated certificate management will experience minimal disruption, as the changes only take effect at certificate renewal after each rollout date. However, administrators must verify that their automation infrastructure can handle more frequent renewals. To address renewal challenges, Let’s Encrypt recommends using ACME Renewal Information (ARI). This feature notifies clients precisely when to renew certificates. For those without ARI support, organizations should implement renewal schedules that renew certificates approximately two thirds of the way through their current validity period. Fixed renewal intervals of 60 days will no longer suffice. The organization is also working with the CA/Browser Forum and the IETF to standardize DNS PERSIST 01, a new validation method that will arrive in 2026. This approach allows administrators to configure DNS entries once without requiring changes at each renewal, significantly simplifying automation for organizations with limited ACME client access to infrastructure. Organizations should implement comprehensive monitoring systems to alert administrators if certificate renewals fail unexpectedly. Let’s Encrypt provides documentation on available monitoring options to help administrators maintain visibility. Administrators can stay informed by subscribing to Let’s Encrypt’s technical updates mailing list. While shorter certificate lifespans require more frequent renewals, the enhanced security posture and new automation tools should significantly reduce operational friction. Encrypt, the nonprofit certificate authority serving millions of websites, announced a significant shift in how it issues digital certificates. </p> <p>Starting in 2026, the organization will reduce the validity period of its <a href="https://gbhackers.com/lets encrypt expands to issue ssl tls certificates/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">SSL/TLS </a>certificates from 90 days to 45 days, with complete implementation expected by February 2028.</p> <p>The move aligns Let’s Encrypt with broader industry standards mandated by the CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements, which establishes technical guidelines for all publicly trusted Certificate Authorities. </p> <p>This industry wide initiative aims to strengthen internet security by limiting the scope of potential compromise and improving the effectiveness of certificate revocation.</p> <p>Beyond shortening certificate lifespans, Let’s Encrypt is also reducing its authorization reuse period from 30 days to just 7 hours by 2028. </p> <p>This means domain control validation will need to occur more frequently. However, the organization is introducing new tools to streamline this process.</p> <h2 class="wp block heading" id="h a-phased rollout to minimize disruption"><strong>A Phased Rollout to Minimize Disruption</strong></h2> <p>Rather than implementing changes overnight, <a href="https://gbhackers.com/lets encrypt to end support/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">Let’s Encrypt</a> will deploy updates across multiple stages using ACME Profiles, which give administrators control over when to adopt new standards. The timeline includes three key milestones.</p> <p>On May 13, 2026, the organization will launch its TLS server ACME profile for early adopters and testing, issuing 45 day certificates. </p> <p>The following year, on February 10, 2027, the default classic profile will issue 64 day certificates with a 10 day authorization reuse period. </p> <p>Finally, on February 16, 2028, the classic profile will fully transition to 45 day certificates with a 7 hour authorization reuse window.</p> <p>Most Let’s Encrypt users with automated <a href="https://gbhackers.com/lets encrypt unveils six day certificate/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">certificate</a> management will experience minimal disruption, as the changes only take effect at certificate renewal after each rollout date. </p> <p>However, administrators must verify that their automation infrastructure can handle more frequent renewals.</p> <p>To address renewal challenges, Let’s Encrypt recommends using ACME Renewal Information (ARI). </p> <p>This feature notifies clients precisely when to renew certificates. For those without ARI support, organizations should implement renewal schedules that renew certificates approximately two thirds of the way through their current validity period. </p> <p>Fixed renewal intervals of 60 days will no longer suffice.</p> <p>The organization is also working with the CA/Browser Forum and the IETF to standardize DNS PERSIST 01, a new validation method that will arrive in 2026. </p> <p>This approach allows administrators to configure DNS entries once without requiring changes at each renewal, significantly simplifying automation for organizations with limited ACME client access to infrastructure.</p> <p>Organizations should implement comprehensive monitoring systems to alert administrators if certificate renewals fail unexpectedly. </p> <p><a href="https://letsencrypt.org/2025/12/02/from 90 to 45.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener nofollow">Let’s Encrypt</a> provides documentation on available monitoring options to help administrators maintain visibility.</p> <p>Administrators can stay informed by subscribing to Let’s Encrypt’s technical updates mailing list. </p> <p>While shorter certificate lifespans require more frequent renewals, the enhanced security posture and new automation tools should significantly reduce operational friction.</p> <p class="has text align center has background" style="background:linear title: Shai-Hulud 2.0 Cyberattack Compromises 30,000 Repos and Exposes 500 GitHub Accounts
raw_text: Shai Hulud 2.0 Cyberattack Compromises 30,000 Repos and Exposes 500 GitHub Accounts gbhackers. Wednesday, December 3, 2025 Linkedin RSS Twitter gbhackers. Home Threats Cyber Attack Data Breach Vulnerability What is DFIR Top 10 Search Follow us On Linkedin Shai Hulud 2.0 Cyberattack Compromises 30,000 Repos and Exposes 500 GitHub Accounts Cyber Attack cyber security Cyber Security News 2 min. Read Shai Hulud 2.0 Cyberattack Compromises 30,000 Repos and Exposes 500 GitHub Accounts By Mayura Kathir December 3, 2025 Share Facebook Twitter Pinterest WhatsApp The Shai Hulud 2.0 supply chain attack has proven to be one of the most persistent and destructive malware campaigns targeting the developer ecosystem. Since the incident first emerged on November 24, 2025, Wiz Research and Wiz CIRT have been tracking the active spread, which continues to evolve, even as infection rates have slowed to a more manageable but still concerning pace. The attack’s scope is staggering. Across the corpus of compromised repositories, Wiz researchers recovered approximately 24,000 unique environment.json files containing critical system and credential information. The malware successfully compromised more than 30,000 total repositories, with roughly 70 percent containing distinct contents representing individual victim environments. Among the most damaging artifacts discovered were over 500 GitHub usernames and tokens exfiltrated from contents.json files. As a result, our response paired the GitHub API with GHArchive, leaving us with one of the most comprehensive data sets on this incident. Pace of the new public repositories. Credentials represent direct access points for further attacks and demonstrate the worm’s sophisticated capability to harvest authentication materials across multiple GitHub accounts and organizations. Shai Hulud 2.0 Cyberattack What distinguishes Shai Hulud 2.0 from previous supply chain worms like s1ngularity and Shai Hulud 1.0 is its remarkable persistence. Six days after initial detection, new repositories continued to be created at a reduced but steady rate. Specifically on CI/CD runners, GitHub Actions is the leading platform with Jenkins, GitLab CI, and AWS CodeBuild coming distant second, third, and fourth. Victim CI/CD platform distribution. A significant resurgence occurred on December 1, 2025, when researchers observed over 200 new infected repositories in just 12 hours, suggesting the attack may experience renewed waves of activity. The malware’s infection methodology reveals strategic sophistication. When unable to locate GitHub credentials locally, the worm searches for previously compromised accounts and uses stolen credentials to upload repositories containing data from new victims. This cross victim exfiltration approach creates a cascading compromise effect that complicates incident response and attribution. While the attack primarily leveraged the npm ecosystem through malicious packages like @postman/tunnel agent and @asyncapi/specs, the compromise extended to multiple software delivery channels. AsyncAPI disclosed that attackers exfiltrated not only npm tokens but also an OpenVSX API key, successfully infecting the AsyncAPI IDE extension and establishing footholds in the OpenVSX ecosystem. asyncapi preview IDE extension. The malware’s reach extended into the Java/Maven ecosystem through automated mirroring mechanisms. Researchers identified the org.mvnpm:posthog node:4.18.1 package as a vector, though active worm spread was not observed in Maven Central or OpenVSX at the time of analysis. Leaked Credentials Pose Active Risk The volume of stolen credentials represents an immediate threat vector for downstream attacks. Analysis revealed that approximately 60 percent of leaked npm tokens remain valid, creating opportunities for attackers to launch additional supply chain campaigns. While truffleSecrets.json files contained up to 400,000 unique secrets, the analysis indicates only about 2.5 percent were verified by the malware, with roughly 25 JWT tokens retaining validity. More troubling is that the threat landscape continues to evolve. Companies have documented confirmed infections through compromised packages, and community response has highlighted persistent confusion about GitHub Actions security controls. Wiz researchers predict continued attacks leveraging similar tactics and procedures, particularly given the vast credential trove already harvested. The Shai Hulud 2.0 incident underscores critical vulnerabilities in supply chain security practices. Organizations must prioritize hardening GitHub Actions configurations, implementing comprehensive secret management strategies, and maintaining vigilant monitoring for compromised credentials. The threat remains active, and the credential cache accumulated during this attack represents a persistent risk for months to come. 20px));max width:none!important}}</style><div class="tdb block inner td fix index"> <p>The Shai Hulud 2.0 supply chain attack has proven to be one of the most persistent and destructive malware campaigns targeting the developer ecosystem. </p> <p>Since the incident first <a href="https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai hulud 2-0 aftermath ongoing supply chain attack" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener nofollow">emerged </a>on November 24, 2025, Wiz Research and Wiz CIRT have been tracking the active spread, which continues to evolve, even as infection rates have slowed to a more manageable but still concerning pace.</p> <p>The attack’s scope is staggering. Across the corpus of compromised repositories, Wiz researchers recovered approximately 24,000 unique environment.json files containing critical system and credential information. </p> <p>The malware successfully compromised more than 30,000 total repositories, with roughly 70 percent containing distinct contents representing individual victim environments.</p> <p>Among the most damaging artifacts discovered were over 500 GitHub usernames and tokens exfiltrated from contents.json files. </p> <p>As a result, our response paired the GitHub API with GHArchive, leaving us with one of the most comprehensive data sets on this incident. </p> <div class="wp block image"> <figure class="aligncenter size large"><img decoding="async" src="https://www.datocms assets.com/75231/1764605985 pace repos.png?fm=webp" alt="Pace of the new public repositories."/><figcaption class="wp element caption">Pace of the new public repositories.</figcaption></figure> </div> <p>Credentials represent direct access points for further attacks and demonstrate the worm’s sophisticated capability to harvest authentication materials across multiple <a href="https://gbhackers.com/github notifications/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">GitHub accounts</a> and organizations.</p> <h2 class="wp block heading" id="h shai hulud 2-0 cyberattack"><strong>Shai Hulud 2.0 Cyberattack </strong></h2> <p>What distinguishes Shai Hulud 2.0 from previous supply chain worms like s1ngularity and Shai Hulud 1.0 is its remarkable persistence. Six days after initial detection, new repositories continued to be created at a reduced but steady rate. </p> <p>Specifically on CI/CD runners, GitHub Actions is the leading platform with Jenkins, GitLab CI, and AWS CodeBuild coming distant second, third, and fourth.</p> <div class="wp block image"> <figure class="aligncenter size large"><img decoding="async" src="https://www.datocms assets.com/75231/1764605630 victimology cicd.png?fm=webp" alt="Victim CI/CD platform distribution."/><figcaption class="wp element caption">Victim CI/CD platform distribution.</figcaption></figure> </div> <p>A significant resurgence occurred on December 1, 2025, when researchers observed over 200 new infected repositories in just 12 hours, suggesting the attack may experience renewed waves of activity.</p> <p>The malware’s infection methodology reveals strategic sophistication. When unable to locate GitHub credentials locally, the worm searches for previously compromised accounts and uses stolen credentials to upload repositories containing data from new victims. </p> <p>This cross victim exfiltration approach creates a cascading compromise effect that complicates incident response and attribution.</p> <p>While the attack primarily leveraged the npm ecosystem through malicious packages like @postman/tunnel agent and @asyncapi/specs, the compromise extended to multiple software delivery channels. </p> <p>AsyncAPI disclosed that attackers exfiltrated not only npm tokens but also an OpenVSX API key, successfully infecting the AsyncAPI IDE extension and establishing footholds in the <a href="https://gbhackers.com/glassworm malware/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">OpenVSX ecosystem</a>.</p> <div class="wp block image"> <figure class="aligncenter size large"><img decoding="async" src="https://www.datocms assets.com/75231/1764584764 asyncapi.png?fm=webp" alt="asyncapi preview IDE extension."/><figcaption class="wp element caption">asyncapi preview IDE extension.</figcaption></figure> </div> <p>The malware’s reach extended into the Java/Maven ecosystem through automated mirroring mechanisms. </p> <p>Researchers identified the org.mvnpm:posthog node:4.18.1 package as a vector, though active worm spread was not observed in Maven Central or OpenVSX at the time of analysis.</p> <h2 class="wp block heading" id="h leaked credentials pose active risk"><strong>Leaked Credentials Pose Active Risk</strong></h2> <p>The volume of stolen credentials represents an immediate threat vector for downstream attacks. </p> <p>Analysis revealed that approximately 60 percent of leaked npm tokens remain valid, creating opportunities for attackers to launch additional <a href="https://gbhackers.com/shai halud targets 477 npm packages/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">supply chain</a> campaigns. </p> <p>While predict continued attacks leveraging similar tactics and procedures, particularly given the vast credential trove already harvested.</p> <p>The Shai Hulud 2.0 incident underscores critical vulnerabilities in supply chain security practices. </p> <p>Organizations must prioritize hardening GitHub Actions configurations, implementing comprehensive secret management strategies, and title: Examining the Risk of AI-Assisted MedusaLocker Ransomware Attacks
raw_text: Examining the Risk of AI Assisted MedusaLocker Ransomware Attacks gbhackers. Wednesday, December 3, 2025 Linkedin RSS Twitter gbhackers. Home Threats Cyber Attack Data Breach Vulnerability What is DFIR Top 10 Search Follow us On Linkedin Examining the Risk of AI Assisted MedusaLocker Ransomware Attacks AI cyber security Cyber Security News 2 min. Read Examining the Risk of AI Assisted MedusaLocker Ransomware Attacks By Mayura Kathir December 3, 2025 Share Facebook Twitter Pinterest WhatsApp Researchers at Cato CTRL have demonstrated that the feature, designed to streamline AI workflows, can be easily weaponized to deploy MedusaLocker ransomware without the user’s knowledge. A new cybersecurity investigation has revealed a critical oversight in Anthropic’s rapidly growing “Claude Skills” ecosystem. Launched in October 2025, Claude Skills enables users to create and share custom code modules to expand AI capabilities. The feature has seen explosive adoption, garnering over 17,000 GitHub stars in just two months. However, Cato CTRL warns that the current permission model creates a dangerous “consent gap.” In a technical breakdown released today, researchers explained that while Claude’s “strict mode” requires users to approve code before execution, this approval provides a false sense of security. Users typically review the visible layer of the script, but once that initial trust is granted, the Skill gains persistent permissions to access the file system and network. To prove the vulnerability, Cato CTRL modified Anthropic’s official open source GIF Creator Skill. They inserted a legitimate looking helper function called post_save. To the user, the script appeared to be standard image processing logic. However, in the background, this function was programmed to fetch and execute external payloads silently. From Productivity to Ransomware In a controlled environment, the researchers utilized this method to execute a live MedusaLocker ransomware attack. The weaponized Skill, once approved by the user, successfully downloaded the malware and encrypted files on the host machine. No secondary prompts, logs, or warnings were triggered during the infection process. “The key issue isn’t that the Skill runs code. It’s that visibility stops at what’s shown,” the Cato CTRL report stated. Execution Flow. “One convincingly packaged malicious Claude Skill, installed and approved once by a single employee, could trigger a multimillion dollar ransomware incident.” With IBM’s 2025 data placing the average cost of a data breach at $5.08 million, the financial implications for Anthropic’s 300,000 business customers are severe. Example of how Claude Skills are shared on social media promising “instant productivity” or viral growth. Malicious actors could easily propagate these weaponized Skills through social engineering on public repositories, disguised as productivity tools. Mitigations Cato CTRL disclosed the vulnerability to Anthropic on October 30, 2025. Cato CTRL advises enterprises to treat AI Skills with the same caution as executable binaries. Recommendations include running Claude code strictly within isolated sandboxes or virtual machines and monitoring for unexpected outbound network connections. Anthropic maintains that the system functions as designed, stating, “It is the user’s responsibility to only use and execute trusted Skills,” and noting that users are explicitly warned that Claude may use instructions and files from the Skill. However, security experts argue that expecting users to audit complex code dependencies is unrealistic. As the ecosystem grows, the line between helpful automation and malware delivery is blurring, requiring a shift in how enterprises trust AI generated code. at Cato CTRL have demonstrated that the feature, designed to streamline AI workflows, can be easily weaponized to deploy MedusaLocker ransomware without the user’s knowledge.</p> <p>A new cybersecurity investigation has <a href="https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato ctrl weaponizing claude skills with medusalocker/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener nofollow">revealed </a>a critical oversight in Anthropic’s rapidly growing “Claude Skills” ecosystem. </p> <p>Launched in October 2025, Claude Skills enables users to create and share custom code modules to expand AI capabilities. </p> <p>The feature has seen explosive adoption, garnering over 17,000 GitHub stars in just two months. However, Cato CTRL warns that the current permission model creates a dangerous “consent gap.”</p> <p>In a technical breakdown released today, researchers explained that while Claude’s “strict mode” requires users to approve code before execution, this approval provides a false sense of security. </p> <p>Users typically review the visible layer of the script, but once that initial trust is granted, the Skill gains persistent permissions to access the file system and network.</p> <p>To prove the vulnerability, Cato CTRL modified Anthropic’s official open source GIF Creator Skill. They inserted a legitimate looking helper function called post_save. </p> <p>To the user, the script appeared to be standard image processing logic. However, in the background, this function was programmed to fetch and execute external payloads silently.</p> <h2 class="wp block heading" id="h from productivity to ransomware"><strong>From Productivity to Ransomware</strong></h2> <p>In a controlled environment, the researchers utilized this method to execute a live MedusaLocker <a href="https://gbhackers.com/colt confirms ransomware attack/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">ransomware attack</a>. </p> <p>The weaponized Skill, once approved by the user, successfully downloaded the malware and encrypted files on the host machine. No secondary prompts, logs, or warnings were triggered during the infection process.</p> <p>“The key issue isn’t that the Skill runs code. It’s that visibility stops at what’s shown,” the Cato CTRL report stated. </p> <div class="wp block image"> <figure class="aligncenter size large"><img decoding="async" src="https://www.catonetworks.com/wp content/uploads/2025/11/fig_3_execution_flow 1536x595.png" alt="Execution Flow."/><figcaption class="wp element caption">Execution Flow.</figcaption></figure> </div> <p>“One convincingly packaged malicious <a href="https://gbhackers.com/claude ai abused in influence as a-service operations/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">Claude Skill</a>, installed and approved once by a single employee, could trigger a multimillion dollar ransomware incident.”</p> <p>With IBM’s 2025 data placing the average cost of a data breach at $5.08 million, the financial implications for Anthropic’s 300,000 business customers are severe. </p> <div class="wp block image"> <figure class="aligncenter size large"><img decoding="async" src="https://www.catonetworks.com/wp content/uploads/2025/11/fig_2_tweet_skill.png.webp" alt="Example of how Claude Skills are shared on social media promising “instant productivity” or viral growth."/><figcaption class="wp element caption"><em><em>Example of how Claude Skills are shared on social media promising “instant productivity” or viral growth.</em></em></figcaption></figure> </div> <p>Malicious actors could easily propagate these weaponized Skills through social engineering on public repositories, disguised as productivity tools.</p> <h2 class="wp block heading" id="h mitigations"><strong>Mitigations</strong></h2> <p>Cato CTRL disclosed the vulnerability to Anthropic on October 30, 2025. </p> <p>Cato CTRL advises enterprises to treat <a href="https://gbhackers.com/creating the perfect blueprint for attackers/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">AI Skills</a> with the same caution as executable binaries. Recommendations include running Claude code strictly within isolated sandboxes or virtual machines and monitoring for unexpected outbound network connections.</p> <p>Anthropic maintains that the system functions as designed, stating, “It is the user’s responsibility to only use and execute trusted Skills,” and noting that users are explicitly warned that Claude may use instructions and files from the Skill.</p> <p>However, security experts argue that expecting users to audit complex code dependencies is unrealistic. </p> <p>As the ecosystem grows, the line between helpful automation and malware delivery is blurring, requiring a shift in how enterprises trust AI generated code.</p> <p class="has text align center has background" style="background:linear title: CISA Issues Alert on Actively Exploited Android Zero-Day Vulnerability
raw_text: CISA Issues Alert on Actively Exploited Android Zero Day Vulnerability gbhackers. Wednesday, December 3, 2025 Linkedin RSS Twitter gbhackers. Read CISA Issues Alert on Actively Exploited Android Zero Day Vulnerability By Mayura Kathir December 3, 2025 Share Facebook Twitter Pinterest WhatsApp The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added two critical Android Framework vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, signaling active exploitation in the wild and prompting immediate action from organizations and device users worldwide. The vulnerabilities CVE 2025 48572 and CVE 2025 48633 were officially listed on December 2, 2025, and represent a significant threat to the millions of Android devices in use across enterprise and consumer environments. CVE 2025 48572 is an Android Framework privilege escalation vulnerability that enables attackers to elevate their access levels on compromised devices. This type of vulnerability is hazardous because it allows threat actors to bypass security restrictions and gain unauthorized control over sensitive system functions. Complementing this threat, CVE 2025 48633 represents an information disclosure vulnerability in the Android Framework, potentially exposing confidential user data and system information to malicious actors. The addition of these vulnerabilities to CISA’s KEV catalog reflects the agency’s commitment to maintaining the authoritative source of actively exploited security vulnerabilities. The KEV catalog serves as a critical resource for network defenders, security professionals, and organizations seeking to prioritize their vulnerability management efforts effectively. By tracking real world exploitation, CISA enables the cybersecurity community to focus remediation resources where they matter most. For organizations managing Android based infrastructure or employee devices, the implications are substantial. Android Zero Day Vulnerability CISA has set a due date of December 23, 2025, for remediation, providing a 21 day window for entities to address the vulnerabilities before mandatory compliance requirements take effect. The agency recommends applying mitigations per vendor instructions as the immediate priority. For those unable to implement patches or mitigations, discontinuing use of affected products may be necessary to prevent compromise. The threat landscape surrounding Android vulnerabilities continues to evolve as attackers increasingly target the platform’s widespread deployment. Android devices manage approximately 70% of the global mobile market share, making them attractive targets for threat actors seeking maximum impact. The combination of privilege escalation and information disclosure vectors creates a compounding threat attackers can exploit these vulnerabilities in sequence to gain complete system control while exfiltrating sensitive data. Organizations should integrate these vulnerabilities into their vulnerability management prioritization frameworks immediately. CISA provides multiple access formats for the KEV catalog including CSV, JSON, and JSON Schema variants enabling seamless integration into security tools and platforms. This accessibility ensures that even organizations with limited resources can leverage CISA’s intelligence to improve their security posture. Recommendations The addition of these Android vulnerabilities reflects broader patterns in the threat landscape, where mobile platforms increasingly become vectors for sophisticated attacks. Enterprise organizations should ensure that Mobile Device Management (MDM) solutions are configured to enforce timely patching and that employees are notified of the importance of accepting security updates promptly. As remediation timelines approach, organizations are encouraged to reference CISA’s advisory guidance and establish clear patching schedules. The KEV catalog, updated continuously as new exploited vulnerabilities emerge, remains an essential tool for defenders seeking to stay ahead of active threat activity. title: Longwatch RCE Flaw Allows Attackers to Run Remote Code with Elevated Privileges
raw_text: Longwatch RCE Flaw Allows Attackers to Run Remote Code with Elevated Privileges gbhackers. Wednesday, December 3, 2025 Linkedin RSS Twitter gbhackers. Home Threats Cyber Attack Data Breach Vulnerability What is DFIR Top 10 Search Follow us On Linkedin Longwatch RCE Flaw CVE/vulnerability Cyber Security News 1 min. Read Longwatch RCE Flaw Allows Attackers to Run Remote Code with Elevated Privileges By Divya December 3, 2025 Share Facebook Twitter Pinterest WhatsApp The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has issued an advisory warning about a critical remote code execution vulnerability affecting Industrial Video & Control’s Longwatch video surveillance and monitoring system. The flaw enables unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code with SYSTEM level privileges, posing significant risks to organizations using the affected platform. Critical Vulnerability Details The vulnerability, identified as CVE 2025 13658, stems from improper control over code generation, allowing attackers to exploit an exposed endpoint via unauthenticated HTTP GET requests. CVE ID CVSS v3.1 Score CVSS v4 Score Severity CVE 2025 13658 9.8 9.3 Critical The security flaw affects Longwatch versions 6.309 through 6.334. It carries a CVSS v3.1 score of 9.8 and a CVSS v4 score of 9.3, both classified as critical severity. The vulnerability is particularly dangerous because it requires no authentication, has low attack complexity, and can be exploited remotely. Successful exploitation grants attackers remote code execution capabilities with elevated SYSTEM level privileges, potentially compromising the entire surveillance infrastructure. The vulnerability impacts critical infrastructure sectors, including Energy, Water, and Wastewater Systems, with deployments worldwide. The absence of code signing and execution controls in the affected versions allows attackers to execute malicious code without proper validation, leading to complete system compromise. Industrial Video & Control strongly recommends that users immediately upgrade to Longwatch version 6.335 or later. CISA advises organizations to minimize network exposure, isolate control systems behind firewalls, and implement secure remote access through updated VPN solutions. Organizations should conduct thorough impact analysis before deploying defensive measures. A concerned OT engineer responsibly disclosed the vulnerability. No public exploitation has been reported to CISA at this time. Follow us on Google News, LinkedIn, and X to Get Instant Updates and Set GBH as a Preferred Source in Google. surveillance and monitoring system. </p> <p>The flaw enables unauthenticated attackers to execute<a href="https://gbhackers.com/watchguard vpn flaw/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener"> arbitrary code</a> with SYSTEM level privileges, posing significant risks to organizations using the affected platform.</p> <h2 class="wp block heading" id="h critical vulnerability details"><strong>Critical Vulnerability Details</strong></h2> <p>The vulnerability, identified as CVE 2025 13658, stems from improper control over code generation, allowing attackers to exploit an exposed endpoint via unauthenticated HTTP GET requests. </p> <figure class="wp block table is style stripes"><table class="has fixed layout"><thead><tr><th class="has text align left" data 13658</td><td>9.8</td><td>9.3</td><td>Critical</td></tr></tbody></table></figure> <p>The security flaw affects Longwatch versions 6.309 through 6.334. It carries a CVSS v3.1 score of 9.8 and a CVSS v4 score of 9.3, both classified as critical severity.</p> <p>The vulnerability is particularly dangerous because it requires no authentication, has low attack complexity, and can be exploited remotely. </p> <p>Successful exploitation grants attackers <a href="https://gbhackers.com/apache tomcat flaws rce/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">remote code execution </a>capabilities with elevated SYSTEM level privileges, potentially compromising the entire surveillance infrastructure.</p> <p>The vulnerability impacts critical infrastructure sectors, including Energy, Water, and Wastewater Systems, with deployments worldwide. </p> <p>The absence of code signing and execution controls in the affected versions allows attackers to execute malicious code without proper validation, leading to complete system compromise.</p> <p>Industrial Video & Control strongly recommends that users immediately upgrade to Longwatch version 6.335 or later. </p> <p>CISA advises organizations to minimize network exposure, isolate control systems behind firewalls, and implement secure remote access through updated VPN solutions. </p> <p>Organizations should conduct thorough impact analysis before deploying defensive measures.</p> <p>A concerned OT engineer responsibly <a href="https://www.cisa.gov/news events/ics advisories/icsa 25 336 01" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener nofollow">disclosed </a>the vulnerability. title: Malicious Rust “evm-units” Impersonator Deploys OS-Specific Payloads
raw_text: Malicious Rust “evm units” Impersonator Deploys OS Specific Payloads gbhackers. Wednesday, December 3, 2025 Linkedin RSS Twitter gbhackers. Home Threats Cyber Attack Data Breach Vulnerability What is DFIR Top 10 Search Follow us On Linkedin Malicious Rust “evm units” Impersonator Deploys OS Specific Payloads cyber security Cyber Security News 3 min. Read Malicious Rust “evm units” Impersonator Deploys OS Specific Payloads By Mayura Kathir December 3, 2025 Share Facebook Twitter Pinterest WhatsApp A malicious Rust crate masquerading as an Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) utility has been caught delivering silent, OS specific payloads to developers’ machines. The package, named evm units and authored by “ablerust,” was hosted on Crates.io for roughly eight months and accumulated over 7,000 all time downloads before being swiftly removed following a report from the Socket Threat Research Team. At first glance, evm units appears to offer a benign helper function, get_evm_version(), returning a plausible EVM version number. Under the hood, however, this call triggers a cross platform second stage loader that fetches and executes a remote payload based on the victim’s operating system and the presence of Qihoo 360 antivirus. Cross platform loader The malicious behavior begins when get_evm_version() is invoked. The function decodes a hardcoded, base64 encoded string into a remote URL, which is then passed into an async check() function. This URL, already flagged as malicious by VirusTotal along with the associated payload hash, serves as the delivery point for the second stage script. The crate implements three OS specific check() variants using Rust’s conditional compilation: On Linux, the malware downloads a script into the system temp directory as /tmp/init, writes the payload to disk, and executes it in the background via nohup bash with all standard streams nulled. No windows, logs, or terminal output alert the victim, while the attacker’s script gains complete control to run arbitrary commands or install additional payloads. On macOS, a similar pattern is used: the payload is saved as init in the temp directory, then quietly executed in the background using osascript wrapped in nohup, again with no visible artifacts to the user. This enables a silent AppleScript based second stage. On Windows, the payload is dropped as a PowerShell script (init.ps1) in the temp directory. The code then enumerates running processes to detect Qihoo 360 (qhsafetray.exe). If Qihoo 360 is absent, the malware generates a VBScript that launches the PowerShell script in a hidden window. Regardless of antivirus presence, it then runs PowerShell with ExecutionPolicy Bypass and CREATE_NO_WINDOW, ensuring stealthy execution. Across all platforms, the use of danger_accept_invalid_certs(true) allows the attacker to use self signed certificates and rotate infrastructure with minimal friction, undermining defensive TLS inspection. Crypto focused supply chain compromise The explicit check for Qihoo 360, a leading Chinese antivirus product with a substantial market share across Asia, points to a likely regional focus and aligns with a cryptocurrency theft profile. The combination of EVM themed utilities, a benign looking Uniswap helper dependency, and cross platform loader behavior strongly suggests targeting of crypto developers or infrastructure. Security teams are urged to treat all open source dependencies as potential attack surfaces, continuously scan for hidden behaviors such as OS specific payload downloads, script execution (PowerShell, Bash, AppleScript), and stealthy initialization hooks, and integrate automated dependency protection into CI/CD pipelines to block malicious crates before they reach production. uniswap utils dependency alert on Socket since it has a dependency containing malware. The risk is amplified by the fact that evm units was not just a standalone crate. Another package by the same author, uniswap utils, appears largely legitimate and has over 7,400 all time downloads. However, it depends on evm units and invokes evm_units::get_evm_version() inside a function annotated with #[ctor::ctor]. This causes the malicious function to run automatically at initialization, turning the incident into a classic software supply chain compromise. This case underscores the growing sophistication of open source malware, especially within cryptocurrency ecosystems. A single seemingly innocuous version check function was enough to conceal a cross platform loader inside widely used Rust crates. width:767px){.tdi_52 img.aligncenter,.tdi_52.aligncenter img{margin left:-20px;width:calc(100% + (2 * 20px));max width:none!important}}</style><div class="tdb block inner td fix index"> <p>A malicious Rust crate masquerading as an Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) utility has been caught delivering silent, OS specific payloads to developers’ machines. </p> <p>The package, named evm units and authored by “ablerust,” was hosted on Crates.io for roughly eight months and accumulated over 7,000 all time downloads before being swiftly removed following a <a href="https://socket.dev/blog/malicious rust crate evm units serves cross platform payloads" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener nofollow">report</a> from the Socket Threat Research Team.</p> <p>At first glance, evm units appears to offer a benign helper function, get_evm_version(), returning a plausible EVM version number. </p> <p>Under the hood, however, this call triggers a cross platform second stage loader that fetches and executes a remote payload based on the victim’s operating system and the presence of Qihoo 360 antivirus.</p> <h2 class="wp block heading" id="h cross platform loader"><strong>Cross platform loader</strong></h2> <p>The malicious behavior begins when get_evm_version() is invoked. The function decodes a hardcoded, base64 encoded string into a remote URL, which is then passed into an async check() function. </p> <p>This URL, already flagged as malicious by <a href="https://gbhackers.com/virustotal launches endpoint/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">VirusTotal</a> along with the associated payload hash, serves as the delivery point for the second stage script.</p> <p>The crate implements three OS specific check() variants using Rust’s conditional compilation:</p> <p>On Linux, the malware downloads a script into the system temp directory as /tmp/init, writes the payload to disk, and executes it in the background via nohup bash with all standard streams nulled. </p> <p>No windows, logs, or terminal output alert the victim, while the attacker’s script gains complete control to run arbitrary commands or install additional payloads.</p> <p>On macOS, a similar pattern is used: the payload is saved as init in the temp directory, then quietly executed in the background using osascript wrapped in nohup, again with no visible artifacts to the user. This enables a silent AppleScript based second stage.</p> <p>On Windows, the payload is dropped as a <a href="https://gbhackers.com/yurei ransomware/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">PowerShell script</a> (init.ps1) in the temp directory. The code then enumerates running processes to detect Qihoo 360 (qhsafetray.exe). </p> <p>If Qihoo 360 is absent, the malware generates a VBScript that launches the PowerShell script in a hidden window. </p> <p>Regardless of antivirus presence, it then runs PowerShell with ExecutionPolicy Bypass and CREATE_NO_WINDOW, ensuring stealthy execution.</p> <p>Across all platforms, the use of danger_accept_invalid_certs(true) allows the attacker to use self signed certificates and rotate infrastructure with minimal friction, undermining defensive TLS inspection.</p> <h2 class="wp block heading" id="h crypto focused supply chain compromise"><strong>Crypto focused supply chain compromise</strong></h2> <p>The explicit check for Qihoo 360, a leading Chinese antivirus product with a substantial market share across Asia, points to a likely regional focus and aligns with a cryptocurrency theft profile. </p> <p>The combination of EVM themed utilities, a benign looking Uniswap helper dependency, and cross platform loader behavior strongly suggests targeting of crypto developers or infrastructure.</p> <p>Security teams are urged to treat all open source dependencies as potential attack surfaces, continuously scan for hidden behaviors such as OS specific payload downloads, script execution (PowerShell, Bash, AppleScript), and stealthy initialization hooks, and integrate automated dependency protection into <a href="https://gbhackers.com/raven vulnerability scanner tool/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">CI/CD pipelines</a> to block malicious crates before they reach production.</p> <div class="wp block image"> <figure class="aligncenter size large"><img decoding="async" src="https://cdn.sanity.io/images/cgdhsj6q/production/5252b65c3a1d141d30d7308d0e98780478f0b4c6 1263x253.png?w=1600&q=95&fit=max&auto=format" alt="uniswap utils dependency alert on Socket since it has a dependency containing malware."/><figcaption class="wp element caption"><em>uniswap utils dependency alert on Socket since it has a dependency containing malware</em>.</figcaption></figure> </div> <p>The risk is amplified by the fact that evm units was not just a standalone crate. Another package by the same author, uniswap utils, appears largely legitimate and has over 7,400 all time downloads.</p> <p>However, it depends on evm units and invokes evm_units::get_evm_version() inside a function annotated with #[ctor::ctor]. This causes the malicious function to run automatically at initialization, turning the incident into a classic software supply chain compromise.</p> <p>This case underscores the growing sophistication of open source malware, especially within cryptocurrency ecosystems. </p> <p>A single seemingly innocuous version check function was enough to conceal a cross platform loader inside widely used Rust crates.</p> <p class="has text align center has background" style="background:linear gradient(135deg,rgb(238,238,238) 100%,rgb(169,184,195) 100%)"><strong>Follow us on <a title: New Calendly-Inspired Phishing Attack Aims to Steal Google Workspace Credentials
raw_text: New Calendly Inspired Phishing Attack Aims to Steal Google Workspace Credentials gbhackers. Wednesday, December 3, 2025 Linkedin RSS Twitter gbhackers. Home Threats Cyber Attack Data Breach Vulnerability What is DFIR Top 10 Search Follow us On Linkedin New Calendly Inspired Phishing Attack Aims to Steal Google Workspace Credentials cyber security Cyber Security News Google 3 min. Read New Calendly Inspired Phishing Attack Aims to Steal Google Workspace Credentials By Mayura Kathir December 3, 2025 Share Facebook Twitter Pinterest WhatsApp A long running phishing campaign is abusing Calendly branded job invitations to compromise Google Workspace and Facebook Business accounts, with a particular focus on hijacking ad management platforms used by agencies and large brands. The operation, uncovered by Push Security, combines Attacker‑in‑the‑Middle (AiTM) and Browser‑in‑the‑Browser (BITB) techniques with targeted controls to evade detection and maximize the value of stolen access. Researchers first observed the campaign after a Push customer was hit with a highly targeted email attack aimed at their Google Workspace account, which served as the organization’s primary identity provider for Google apps and downstream single sign on. Despite the breadth of access a compromised Google Workspace The initial lure in this case was framed as a job opportunity with LVMH, sent from an address impersonating “Inside LVMH,” the group’s talent acquisition and training arm. After entering an allowed email domain, the password entry field loads. The email was well written, tailored with victim specific details, and appeared to come from a legitimate employee whose identity could be easily verified via open source searches. Phishing Pages Capture Google Workspace Logins Push Security assesses it is plausible that generative AI and web scraped data were used to craft these convincing exchanges. Critically, the phishing link was only delivered after an initial back and forth, embedded as a Calendly style link to “book time for a call.” This multi stage choreography is designed to slip past email security tools tuned to scan for embedded links and urgent calls to action. Clicking the link sends victims to a fake Calendly landing page, complete with CAPTCHA, before presenting a “Continue with Google” option. Fake Calendly landing page. From there, the victim is redirected into an AiTM phishing page that proxies the real Google login flow while displaying Calendly branding, making it visually distinct from more common Google themed phishing kits. The page uses conditional loading and domain based checks to ensure only the intended organization’s email domains can proceed. Attempts to log in with other domains are blocked, preventing security analysts and automated scanners from easily observing the credential harvesting logic. Pages with similar properties impersonating Unilever, Disney, Lego, Artisan, and many more brands. Push Security identified numerous related pages sharing the same Calendly themed design, impersonating recruiters or HR staff at LVMH, Lego, Mastercard, Uber, and other major brands. Spot and Stop These Imitation Invite Attacks A second variant, dating back more than two years, targets Facebook Business accounts via similar themed pages, with at least 31 unique URLs being recycled over time to impersonate different companies. A newer third variant blends both approaches, targeting Google and Facebook accounts via Calendly styled pages that spawn a BITB pop up. BITB style pop up window showing a legitimate looking URL. This technique masks the actual phishing server behind a fake, attacker controlled URL bar inside the pop up, further eroding users’ ability to distinguish real login prompts from malicious overlays. Additional anti analysis checks including IP based blocking and triggers tied to accessing browser developer tools make these pages even harder for defenders to investigate. The strategic focus on business ad management accounts aligns with broader shifts in the threat landscape. Compromised Google Ads and Facebook Business accounts can be weaponized to run malvertising campaigns that distribute AiTM phishing, malware, and advanced “ClickFix” scams at scale, while sidestepping traditional email based protections. With ad platforms offering fine grained targeting by geography, domain, and device type, attackers can blend wide net credential harvesting with precise targeting of high value organizations. By starting with identity based initial access via Google Workspace and then pivoting into ad infrastructure, the operators behind this Calendly themed campaign are positioning themselves to both monetize and operationalize stolen access either directly, through malicious ad buys, or indirectly, by selling footholds to other criminal groups. 20px));max width:none!important}}</style><div class="tdb block inner td fix index"> <p>A long running phishing campaign is abusing Calendly branded job invitations to compromise Google Workspace and Facebook Business accounts, with a particular focus on hijacking ad management platforms used by agencies and large brands. </p> <p>The operation, <a href="https://pushsecurity.com/blog/uncovering a-calendly themed phishing campaign" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener nofollow">uncovered</a> by Push Security, combines Attacker‑in‑the‑Middle (AiTM) and Browser‑in‑the‑Browser (BITB) techniques with targeted controls to evade detection and maximize the value of stolen access.</p> <p>Researchers first observed the campaign after a Push customer was hit with a highly targeted email attack aimed at their Google Workspace account, which served as the organization’s primary identity provider for Google apps and downstream single sign on. </p> <p>Despite the breadth of access a compromised <a href="https://gbhackers.com/google workspace announced new password policies/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">Google Workspace </a>account would provide, the attacker’s apparent priority was seizing control of accounts used to manage digital advertising.</p> <p>The initial lure in this case was framed as a job opportunity with LVMH, sent from an address impersonating “Inside LVMH,” the group’s talent acquisition and training arm. </p> <div class="wp block image"> <figure class="aligncenter size large"><img decoding="async" src="https://images.ctfassets.net/y1cdw1ablpvd/5JzkZirFB5VsTMbf9nlX58/6d7f6d72465df9c0133044bce33c6de1/image1.png" alt="After entering an allowed email domain, the password entry field loads."/><figcaption class="wp element caption">After entering an allowed email domain, the password entry field loads.</figcaption></figure> </div> <p>The email was well written, tailored with victim specific details, and appeared to come from a legitimate employee whose identity could be easily verified via open source searches. </p> <h2 class="wp block heading" id="h phishing pages capture google workspace logins"><strong>Phishing Pages Capture Google Workspace Logins</strong></h2> <p>Push Security assesses it is plausible that generative AI and web scraped data were used to craft these convincing exchanges.</p> <p>Critically, the phishing link was only delivered after an initial back and forth, embedded as a Calendly style link to “book time for a call.” </p> <p>This multi stage choreography is designed to slip past email security tools tuned to scan for embedded links and urgent calls to action. </p> <p>Clicking the link sends victims to a fake Calendly landing page, complete with CAPTCHA, before presenting a “Continue with Google” option.</p> <div class="wp block image"> <figure class="aligncenter size large"><img decoding="async" src="https://images.ctfassets.net/y1cdw1ablpvd/4YX3lqU3K4EVv230yAXPLu/1d640fd64d2db7b55b64828e02bb244b/Group_584.png" alt="Fake Calendly landing page."/><figcaption class="wp element caption">Fake Calendly landing page.</figcaption></figure> </div> <p>From there, the victim is redirected into an <a href="https://gbhackers.com/banking aitm phishing/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">AiTM phishing page</a> that proxies the real Google login flow while displaying Calendly branding, making it visually distinct from more common Google themed phishing kits. </p> <p>The page uses conditional loading and domain based checks to ensure only the intended organization’s email domains can proceed. </p> <p>Attempts to log in with other domains are blocked, preventing security analysts and automated scanners from easily observing the credential harvesting logic.</p> <div class="wp block image"> <figure class="aligncenter size large"><img decoding="async" src="https://images.ctfassets.net/y1cdw1ablpvd/6rzP1eIMjdI6rCPTQEQvMe/a57c25f26f5ff9e38e1ecfbe47a5e039/image6.png" alt="Pages with similar properties impersonating Unilever, Disney, Lego, Artisan, and many more brands."/><figcaption class="wp element caption">Pages with similar properties impersonating Unilever, Disney, Lego, Artisan, and many more brands.</figcaption></figure> </div> <p>Push Security identified numerous related pages sharing the same Calendly themed design, impersonating recruiters or HR staff at LVMH, Lego, Mastercard, Uber, and other major brands. </p> <h2 class="wp block heading" id="h spot and stop these imitation invite attacks"><strong>Spot and Stop These Imitation Invite Attacks</strong></h2> <p>A second variant, dating back more than two years, targets Facebook Business accounts via similar themed pages, with at least 31 unique URLs being recycled over time to impersonate different companies.</p> <p>A newer third variant blends both approaches, targeting Google and Facebook accounts via Calendly styled pages that spawn a BITB pop up. </p> <div class="wp block image"> <figure class="aligncenter size large"><img decoding="async" src="https://images.ctfassets.net/y1cdw1ablpvd/4oeu6wp1oKSHblbVf6M2vN/a29ce019b7f5e40eb8017c3a28553457/image2.png" alt="BITB style pop up window showing a legitimate looking URL."/><figcaption class="wp element caption">BITB style pop up window showing a legitimate looking URL.</figcaption></figure> </div> <p>This technique masks the actual phishing server behind a fake, attacker controlled URL bar inside the pop up, further eroding users’ ability to distinguish real login prompts from malicious overlays. </p> <p>Additional anti analysis checks including IP based blocking and triggers tied to accessing browser developer tools make these pages even harder for defenders to investigate.</p> <p>The strategic focus on business ad management accounts aligns with broader shifts in the threat landscape. </p> <p>Compromised <a href="https://gbhackers.com/gootloader malware spreads via google ads/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">Google Ads </a>and Facebook Business accounts can be weaponized to run malvertising campaigns that distribute AiTM phishing, malware, and advanced “ClickFix” scams at scale, while sidestepping traditional email based protections. </p> <p>With ad platforms offering fine grained targeting by geography, domain, and device type, attackers can blend wide net credential harvesting with precise targeting of high value organizations.</p> <p>By starting with identity based initial access via Google Workspace and then pivoting into ad infrastructure, the operators behind this Calendly themed campaign are positioning themselves to both monetize and operationalize stolen access either directly, through malicious ad buys, or indirectly, by selling footholds to other criminal groups.</p> <p class="has text align center has background" Home Threats Cyber Attack Data Breach Vulnerability What is DFIR Top 10 Search Follow us On Linkedin Threat Actors Using Matanbuchus Downloader to Deliver Ransomware and Maintain Persistence cyber security Cyber Security News Ransomware 3 min. Read Threat Actors Using Matanbuchus Downloader to Deliver Ransomware and Maintain Persistence By Mayura Kathir December 3, 2025 Share Facebook Twitter Pinterest WhatsApp Threat actors are increasingly abusing the Matanbuchus malicious downloader as a key enabler for hands on keyboard ransomware operations, using its backdoor like capabilities to deliver secondary payloads, move laterally, and maintain long term persistence on compromised systems. Initially observed in 2020 and offered as Malware as a-Service (MaaS), Matanbuchus has steadily evolved, with version 3.0 identified in the wild in July 2025, introducing more sophisticated network serialization and encryption features. Matanbuchus is written in C++ and primarily functions as a downloader and backdoor, designed to fetch and execute additional payloads. It consists of two main components: a dedicated downloader module and a main module. The downloader retrieves and launches the main module, which, in turn, provides a flexible command and control (C2) framework that enables threat actors to execute binaries, scripts, shellcode, and even.NET payloads directly in memory. This flexibility has made Matanbuchus increasingly attractive to ransomware operators seeking reliable initial access tooling and post exploitation control. Recent activity observed by Zscaler ThreatLabz highlights a campaign in which attackers used Microsoft’s QuickAssist, likely combined with social engineering, to gain remote access to victim systems. Once access was established, the threat actor executed a malicious Microsoft Installer (MSI) package from a compromised domain, which delivered an executable that sideloaded a malicious DLL. Overview of Matanbuchus Malware This DLL acted as the Matanbuchus downloader, pulling the main module from a remote C2 endpoint. ThreatLabz assesses with medium confidence that these actions were part of a broader ransomware deployment chain. Matanbuchus employs extensive obfuscation and anti analysis mechanisms to evade detection and hinder reverse engineering. Strings are stored in encrypted form and decrypted at runtime using the ChaCha20 stream cipher, with encrypted strings and metadata organized in dedicated arrays. Windows API functions are resolved dynamically via MurmurHash based hashing, and the codebase is interspersed with junk instructions to frustrate static analysis. Example of junk instructions in the Matanbuchus main module code. The downloader further incorporates long running “busy” loops to delay execution by several minutes, attempting to run past typical sandbox timeouts. Network communication is equally hardened. The downloader includes embedded encrypted shellcode that is decrypted using a brute force known plaintext technique against ChaCha20 keys constructed from a decrementing integer seed. Example of junk code and long running busy loops in the Matanbuchus downloader module. Once decrypted, this shellcode downloads the main module over HTTPS and decrypts it using ChaCha20, chunked in blocks to process large payloads efficiently. With version 3.0, Matanbuchus adopted Protocol Buffers (Protobufs) to serialize its C2 messages, wrapping encrypted Protobuf data in custom packets that prepend a random key and nonce for each request. After deployment, the main module registers the compromised host with the C2 server, exfiltrating host and user information, including hostname, username, Windows version and domain, installed security products (such as EDR and XDR solutions), OS architecture, and privilege level. Mitigations It then writes a registry marker under the current user hive to track registration state and establishes persistence by executing C2 delivered shellcode that creates a scheduled task named “Update Tracker Task.” Matanbuchus network communication pattern. This task launches msiexec.exe with parameters pointing to a randomly named copy of the malware stored in a uniquely generated directory under the APPDATA folder, tied to the system’s volume serial number. From there, Matanbuchus acts as a full featured backdoor. It supports commands to download and run EXEs, DLLs, MSI packages, and shellcode; enumerate processes, services, software, and Windows updates; run system commands via CMD, PowerShell, or WMI; and even terminate itself. ThreatLabz has also documented campaigns where Matanbuchus was used to distribute the Rhadamanthys information stealer and the NetSupport RAT, underscoring its role as a versatile delivery platform. Coupled with observed hands on keyboard activity and a growing association with ransomware affiliates, Matanbuchus represents a mature, evolving MaaS capability that significantly lowers the barrier for conducting complex intrusion and extortion operations. 20px));max width:none!important}}</style><div class="tdb block inner td fix index"> <p>Threat actors are increasingly abusing the Matanbuchus malicious downloader as a key enabler for hands on keyboard ransomware operations, using its backdoor like capabilities to deliver secondary payloads, move laterally, and maintain long term persistence on compromised systems. </p> <p>Initially <a href="https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security research/technical analysis matanbuchus 3-0" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener nofollow">observed </a>in 2020 and offered as Malware as a-Service (MaaS), Matanbuchus has steadily evolved, with version 3.0 identified in the wild in July 2025, introducing more sophisticated network serialization and encryption features.</p> <p>Matanbuchus is written in C++ and primarily functions as a downloader and backdoor, designed to fetch and execute additional payloads. </p> <p>It consists of two main components: a dedicated downloader module and a main module. The downloader retrieves and launches the main module, which, in turn, provides a flexible command and control (C2) framework that enables threat actors to execute binaries, scripts, shellcode, and even.NET payloads directly in memory. </p> <p>This flexibility has made Matanbuchus increasingly attractive to ransomware operators seeking reliable initial access tooling and post exploitation control.</p> <p>Recent activity observed by Zscaler ThreatLabz highlights a campaign in which attackers used Microsoft’s QuickAssist, likely combined with social engineering, to gain remote access to victim systems. </p> <p>Once access was established, the threat actor executed a malicious <a href="https://gbhackers.com/new stealc v2 upgrade targets microsoft installer packages/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">Microsoft Installer</a> (MSI) package from a compromised domain, which delivered an executable that sideloaded a malicious DLL. </p> <h2 class="wp block heading" id="h overview of matanbuchus malware"><strong>Overview of Matanbuchus Malware</strong></h2> <p>This DLL acted as the Matanbuchus downloader, pulling the main module from a remote C2 endpoint. ThreatLabz assesses with medium confidence that these actions were part of a broader ransomware deployment chain.</p> <p>Matanbuchus employs extensive obfuscation and anti analysis mechanisms to evade detection and hinder reverse engineering. </p> <p>Strings are stored in encrypted form and decrypted at runtime using the ChaCha20 stream cipher, with encrypted strings and metadata organized in dedicated arrays. </p> <p>Windows API functions are resolved dynamically via MurmurHash based hashing, and the codebase is interspersed with junk instructions to frustrate static analysis. </p> <div class="wp block image"> <figure class="aligncenter size large"><img decoding="async" src="https://cms.zscaler.com/cdn cgi/image/format=auto/sites/default/files/images/blogs/Figure%201.png" alt="Example of junk instructions in the Matanbuchus main module code."/><figcaption class="wp element caption">Example of junk instructions in the Matanbuchus main module code.</figcaption></figure> </div> <p>The downloader further incorporates long running “busy” loops to delay execution by several minutes, attempting to run past typical sandbox timeouts.</p> <p>Network communication is equally hardened. The downloader includes embedded encrypted shellcode that is decrypted using a brute force known plaintext technique against ChaCha20 keys constructed from a decrementing integer seed. </p> <div class="wp block image"> <figure class="aligncenter size large"><img decoding="async" src="https://cms.zscaler.com/cdn cgi/image/format=auto/sites/default/files/images/blogs/Figure%202.png" alt="Example of junk code and long running busy loops in the Matanbuchus downloader module."/><figcaption class="wp element caption">Example of junk code and long running busy loops in the Matanbuchus downloader module.</figcaption></figure> </div> <p>Once decrypted, this shellcode downloads the main module over HTTPS and decrypts it using ChaCha20, chunked in blocks to process large payloads efficiently. </p> <p>With version 3.0, Matanbuchus adopted Protocol Buffers (Protobufs) to serialize its C2 messages, wrapping encrypted Protobuf data in custom packets that prepend a random key and nonce for each request.</p> <p>After deployment, the main module registers the compromised host with the <a href="https://gbhackers.com/open source package/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">C2 server</a>, exfiltrating host and user information, including hostname, username, Windows version and domain, installed security products (such as EDR and XDR solutions), OS architecture, and privilege level. </p> <h2 class="wp block heading" id="h mitigations"><strong>Mitigations</strong></h2> <p>It then writes a registry marker under the current user hive to track registration state and establishes persistence by executing C2 delivered shellcode that creates a scheduled task named “Update Tracker Task.” </p> <div class="wp block image"> <figure class="aligncenter size large"><img decoding="async" src="https://cms.zscaler.com/cdn cgi/image/format=auto/sites/default/files/images/blogs/final_diagram.png" alt="Matanbuchus network communication pattern."/><figcaption class="wp element caption">Matanbuchus network communication pattern.</figcaption></figure> </div> <p>This task launches msiexec.exe with parameters pointing to a randomly named copy of the malware stored in a uniquely generated directory under the APPDATA folder, tied to the system’s volume serial number.</p> <p>From there, Matanbuchus acts as a full featured backdoor. It supports commands to download and run EXEs, DLLs, <a href="https://gbhackers.com/hackers weaponize msi packages png files to deliver multi stage malware/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">MSI packages</a>, and shellcode; enumerate processes, services, software, and Windows updates; run system commands via CMD, PowerShell, or WMI; and even terminate itself. </p> <p>ThreatLabz has also documented campaigns where Matanbuchus was used to distribute the Rhadamanthys information stealer and the NetSupport RAT, underscoring its role as a versatile delivery platform. </p> <p>Coupled with observed hands on keyboard activity and a growing association with ransomware affiliates, Matanbuchus represents a mature, evolving MaaS capability that significantly lowers the barrier for conducting complex intrusion and extortion operations.</p> <h2 class="wp block heading" id="h indicators of compromise iocs"><strong>Indicators Of Compromise (IOCs)</strong></h2> <figure title: Google expands Android scam protection feature to Chase, Cash App in U.S.

Google expands Android scam protection feature to Chase, Cash App in U.S. Home News Security Google expands Android scam protection feature to Chase, Cash App in U.S. Google expands Android scam protection feature to Chase, Cash App in U.S. By Bill Toulas December 3, 2025 12:00 PM 0 Google is expanding support for its Android's in call scam protection to multiple banks and financial applications in the United States. The announcement specifically mentions the addition of fintech app Cash App, which has 57 million users, and the JPMorganChase mobile banking app, which has more than 50 million downloads on Google Play. In call scam protection is a new feature that was announced in May and introduced in Android 16, Its purpose is to warn users of a potential danger when they launch a financial app and are sharing their screen while in a call with an unknown number. Google says that this security feature defends against a popular scam where cybercriminals are "impersonating banks or other trusted institutions on the phone to try to manipulate victims into sharing their screen in order to reveal banking information or make a financial transfer." In this scenario, an alert is shown, informing the user that the caller may be an impersonator and that the instructions they convey should be ignored. The user is also advised not to share any information or make any payments. The warning pop up persists for 30 seconds and the only option is to end the call. Google notes that the 30 second pause should break the attacker's social engineering "spell," and disrupt the false sense of urgency and panic that are required for the scam to be successful. The warning message Source: Google The in call scam protection system only works on Android 11 and later and started as a trial in the U.K., where apps from most major banks are enrolled. After helping "thousands of users end calls that could have cost them a significant amount of money," the company expanded the pilot with financial apps in Brazil and India. Today, the system expands to U.S., where users of several popular fintech and bank apps, among them CashApp and JPMorgan Chase, are supported. The protection system continues to run in testing phase. Users should be aware of risky actions required of them from unknown callers, such as installing APKs from unofficial sources, granting accessibility permissions to malware apps, and disabling Play Protect on the device. As part of good security practices, users should avoid sharing personal information with unknown callers and never jump into action before confirming the status of their accounts by contacting their bank directly. By
Bill Toulas
